Since G_C, M_C are of the same complex dimension, and the map A_v is G_C equivariant, Sard's theorem says that every point in M_C is a regular value of A_v, and hence, A_v is a topological covering. If v in M, the covering A_v: G to M is a diffeomorphism. Since the inclusions G subset G_C, M subset M_C are homotopy equivalences, the covering A_v has degree 1 over all of M_C, and therefore A_v is a global biholomorphism. vskip 2mm vskip 2mm To show that G_C acts locally transitively, it suffices to show that \[ DA_v: T^1,0_I G_C = g_C to T_v^1,0 M_C \] is an isomorphism. By lemma \ref{lemma:action}, we know that $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$. We will prove that it acts locally transitively at every point $v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$. Assuming this for the moment, this proves that all orbits of $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are open, and since $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ is connected, this proves that the mapping $A_v: G_{\mathbb{C}} \ni h \to h\cdot v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$, for any fixed $v \in M_{\mathbb{C}}$, is surjective. Since $G_{\mathbb{C}}, M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are of the same complex dimension, and the map $A_v$ is $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ equivariant, Sard's theorem says that every point in $M_{\mathbb{C}}$ is a regular value of $A_v$, and hence, $A_v$ is a topological covering. If $v \in M$, the covering $A_v: G \to M$ is a diffeomorphism. Since the inclusions $G \subset G_{\mathbb{C}}, M \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$ are homotopy equivalences, the covering $A_v$ has degree 1 over all of $M_{\mathbb{C}}$, and therefore $A_v$ is a global biholomorphism.

\vskip 2mm
To show that $G_{\mathbb{C}}$ acts locally transitively, it suffices to show that 

\[
	DA_{v}: T^{1,0}_{I} G_{\mathbb{C}} = \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} \to T_v^{1,0} M_{\mathbb{C}}
\]

is an isomorphism. This, in turn is equivalent to showing that, for a basis $\xi_1, \xi_2,\ldots, \xi_n$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ over $\mathbb{R}$, the complex fields $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2, \ldots, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n$ are a basis for $T^{1,0}M_{\mathbb{C}}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ at $v$. Define $\mathcal{P} = \{ \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1 \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2 \wedge \ldots \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n = 0\}$. We wish to show $\mathcal{P}$ is empty. 

\vskip 2mm

Assume it is not empty. Then $\mathcal{P}$ is a $G_{\mathbb{C}}$-invariant divisor on $M_{\mathbb{C}}$, and $\mathcal{P} \cap M = \emptyset$. Consider the plurisubharmonic function $u$ restricted to $\mathcal{P}$. Since $u$ is non-negative and proper when restricted to $\mathcal{P}$, it achieves a global minimum at some $v \in \mathcal{P}$. The map $A_v$ restricted to $G$ gives an embedding of $G$ into $\mathcal{P} \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$ where it is a $CR$-submanifold of real dimension $n$. Note that the function $u$ is constant on $S_v := A_v(G)$. Since $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} \mathcal{P} < n$, $S_v$ cannot be a totally real submanifold in $\mathcal{P}$. Hence its complex tangent space is positive dimensional at every point. Its Levi-form cannot be trivial, since otherwise the leaves of the Levi foliation of $S_v$ would give positive-dimensional complex submanifolds in the level set $\{u = u(v)\}$, which is strictly pseudoconvex, by the tube construction. By a classical construction in complex analysis (local Bishop disks), there exists a continuous mapping $F: \bar{\triangle} \to U \subset M_{\mathbb{C}}$, where $U$ is a small polydisk neighborhood of $v$, and with $F|_{\triangle}$ holomorphic and non-constant, and $F(\partial \triangle) \subset S_v$. Thus $u\circ F|_{\partial\triangle} \equiv u(v)$. Therefore, $F(\triangle) \subset \mathcal{P} \cap U$, since $\mathcal{P} \cap U$ is closed and analytic in $U$, which gives us that $u\circ F(z) \geq u(v),$ for all $z \in \triangle$. By the maximum principle, $u\circ F$ is constant on $\triangle$, contradicting, again, the strict pseudoconvexity of $S_v$.

\[
\begin{array}{rcl}

	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_1 \, \lambda_3 \,(\lambda_3 - \lambda_1)\, z_1\, z_3 \\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_2 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_2)\, z_2 \, z_3 \\

	0 & = & \lambda_1\, (b - \lambda_1 \, a) \, z_1 \, w\\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_2 \, (b - \lambda_2 \, a) \, z_2 \, w \\
	\\
	0 & = & \lambda_3 \, (b - \lambda_3 \, a) \, z_3 \, w.
\end{array}
\]

nodes.statement: This is an immediate consequence of a result of SzHoke (cf also ). The metric () has an isometry group G times S^1 where the factor S^1 acts by right multiplication on G by the 1-parameter subgroup e^t\, xi_3 on the right, i.e., by R_e^t\, xi_3, periodic of period 2pi, and the factor G acts by left multiplication L_g on G. Consider the manifold G times S^1, where G is given the bi-invariant metric of sectional curvature 1, which is the special case of () with lambda_1= 1, and the S^1 factor is given the metric mu dtheta^2, where dtheta^2 is the invariant metric of length 2pi on S^1 and mu is a real constant > 0. So Gtimes S^1 has the metric g_mu defined by g_mu = g_I oplus mu \, dtheta^2. Consider the quotient manifold of Gtimes S^1 by the action of S^1 = \e^i t\ on Gtimes S^1 given by e^i t cdot (g, e^i theta) = (gcdot e^2 t\, xi_3, e^i(theta + t)). Then it is easy to see that the quotient manifold Gtimes S^1/sim is diffeomorphic to G. Let barg_mu be the Riemannian submersion metric from (). By construction, this metric is invariant under left translation by G and by right translation by e^- t \, xi_3. Consequently, it is one of the left invariant metrics on G with an extra isometric action from the right. It is an easy calculation to see which ones arise in this manner. Let A = left(ccc 1 & & \\ & 1 & \\ & & lambda right). Explicitly, we will normalize our metrics so that g_A(xi_1, xi_1) = g_A(xi_2, xi_2) = frac14, and g_A(xi_3, xi_3) = fraclambda4.footnoteThis means that instead of g_A(cdot,cdot) = -B(A(cdot), cdot), we now have g_A(cdot, cdot) = -frac18 B(A(cdot), cdot). With this normalization, the case A = I gives the round metric with sectional curvature K = 1 on G cong S^3. vskip 2mm We want to see which lambda in () will arise from SzHoke's construction. Computing at (e,1) in Gtimes S^1, the tangent vector to the S^1 action we will quotient by is given by (2xi_3, fracpartial \;\;partial theta). Let $\gamma$ be the real geodesic on $G$ with initial conditions $\gamma(0) = e \in G$ and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = v_0 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$. We solve the geodesic equations (\ref{eqn:geodeqns1}) in the appendix \cite{web} relatively explicitly to show that the complexified geodesic $\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}(\zeta)$ is an entire function from $\mathbb{C}$ to $G_{\mathbb{C}}$. The other statements in the proposition follow from smooth dependence on initial conditions.
\vskip 2mm
For convenience, we repeat here the equations (\ref{eqn:geodeqns1}) from \cite{web} for the tangent vector $T = a\, \xi_1+b\, \xi_2+c\, \xi_3$ to a geodesic, subject to the initial condition $T(0) = a_0 \, \xi_1+ b_0\, \xi_2 +c_0 \, \xi_3,$ for a metric of the form $g_A$,  with $A$ as in (\ref{eqn:A}):
\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		\dot{a} & = & -b\, c\, (\lambda - 1) \\
		&&\\
		\dot{b} & = & - a\, c\, (1 - \lambda) \\
		&&\\
		\dot{c} & = & 0,
	\end{array}
\]


where $\dot{a} = T(a)$, etc. We get that $c \equiv c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and the system reduces to 


\[
	\begin{array}{rcr}
		\dot{a} & = & -\nu\, b \\
		&&\\
		\dot{b} & = & \nu \, a, 
	\end{array}
\]


with $\nu = c_0 \, (\lambda - 1) \in \mathbb{R}$. Hence, 

\vskip 2mm

\[
	\begin{array}{rcl} a & \equiv & a_0 \cos \nu \, t - b_0 \sin \nu \,t \\&&\\ b & \equiv & b_0 \cos \nu \,t + a_0 \sin \nu \, t, \end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm
where $t$ is the parameter of integration in the equations. Set 

\[
	T_{\mathbb{C}} = a(\zeta) \, \xi_{1,\mathbb{C}} +b(\zeta) \, \xi_{2,\mathbb{C}} + c_0 \, \xi_{3,\mathbb{C}},
\] 

which is an entire function from $\mathbb{C} \to \mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C}) \subset \mathbb{C}^4.$ Considering $\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}$ as a function from, at first, a neighborhood of $\mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}$ to $G_{\mathbb{C}} = SL(2,\mathbb{C}) \subset \mathbb{C}^4$, we have that it satisfies the equation 

\[
	\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}(\zeta)^{-1} \cdot \dot{\gamma_{\mathbb{C}}} = T_{\mathbb{C}},
\]

where $\dot{\gamma}_{\mathbb{C}} = \frac{d\;\;}{d \zeta}$, since we are using the left-invariant parallelism to trivialize $T^{1,0}G_{\mathbb{C}}$. Equivalently, we have

\[
	  \dot{\gamma}_{\mathbb{C}} = \gamma_{\mathbb{C}} \cdot T_{\mathbb{C}},
	 \]
	 
which is a linear equation, with $T_{\mathbb{C}}$ entire and known, on all of $\mathbb{C}$. Hence all its solutions extend to entire functions, proving the lemma.

By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to \vskip 2mm
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		
		\item Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mathfrak{g}$.\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		
		\item Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vskip 2mm 
			\begin{equation}\label{eqn:Yinit}
				\left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\mathcal{F}_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right).
			\end{equation}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		\item Express $Y_{i,\mathbb{C}} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\mathbb{C}}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm
		
		\item Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$.
	\end{enumerate}\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm

We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition.

\vskip 2mm\vskip 2mm

Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}):
	
	\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\mathbb{H} & = &  b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, 
	\end{array}
	\]

where $a, b, c ,d \in \mathbb{R}$. (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say

\vskip 2mm

\[
\begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\mathbb{H}'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm
and

\vskip 2mm

	\[
	\begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array}
	\]
	
	\vskip 2mm
Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have

\vskip 2mm

\begin{equation}\label{eqn:fhsols}
		\left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\  \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right).
\end{equation}


\vskip 2mm


As to step (3), as  in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly:

\vskip 2mm

\[
	\begin{array}{rcccl}
		\eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\
			&&&&\\
		\eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3.
	\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm

so that we have 


\vskip 2mm


\[
	\begin{array}{rcl}
		\left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot  \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\  \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\
		& = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin  t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). 
	\end{array}
\]

\vskip 2mm

It follows directly that

\vskip 2mm

\[ 
	Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right).
\]

\vskip 2mm

Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if 

\vskip 2mm

\begin{equation}\label{eqn:tstar}
	\frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t.
\end{equation}

\vskip 2mm

It is clear pictorially or from an elementary calculus computation that, if $\lambda >1$, there is a unique $t_*(\lambda) > 0$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:tstar}), as claimed
